title: Australia's 'most haunted' estate hits the market for $1.9million
excerpt: One of Australia's most 'haunted' homes is on the market for $1.9million, offering prospective buyers the chance to own a magnificent historic estate with a rather unsettling reputation.
content:
One of Australia's most notoriously 'haunted' homes is on the market for $1.9million, offering prospective buyers the chance to own a magnificent historic estate with a rather unsettling reputation.

Monte Cristo Homestead, located at 1 Homestead Lane in the NSW Riverina town of Junee, has attracted paranormal enthusiasts for decades, with visitors reporting everything from mysterious figures appearing in bedrooms to unexplained voices and objects moving on their own.

But beyond the ghost stories lies a grand 19th-century residence set across six acres, complete with a ballroom, stables, a swimming pool, sweeping balconies and an extraordinary collection of antique furniture and artwork.

The 18-bedroom property is being sold on a walk-in, walk-out basis, meaning its new owners will inherit the contents of the historic home, which have been collected over decades.

Real estate agent Jason Barrett told the Daily Mail that the homestead offers a rare opportunity to buyers.

'This is more than just a home - it is a landmark, a story, and an opportunity to own a true piece of Australian history,' he said.

The sale has also attracted attention online, where Australians have suggested transforming the estate into a boutique accommodation venue for those brave enough to spend the night.

'This is a PSA that Australia's most haunted house is currently up for sale. I need someone to buy it and restore it and put it up as an Airbnb,' creator Hannah said in a video.

The fascinating history behind Monte Cristo Homestead

The property's history dates back to 1885, when wealthy landowner Christopher Crawley and his wife Elizabeth established the grand family residence.

Mr Crawley owned more than 500 acres of land on which the town of Junee now stands and made his fortune after establishing a pub opposite the newly built railway station.

He poured his wealth into constructing Monte Cristo, meaning 'Mount of Christ', selecting a prominent position overlooking his vast landholding.

The estate became a setting for lavish social gatherings, with its ballroom and expansive grounds reflecting the family's wealth and standing within the community.

However, following Christopher's death at the property in 1910, aged 69, his widow reportedly became increasingly reclusive.

Elizabeth is believed to have left the property on just two occasions during the remaining 23 years of her life, converting an upstairs room into a private chapel and devoting herself to her faith.

She died at the homestead in 1933, aged 92.

The last members of the Crawley family vacated the property in 1948, leaving it vulnerable to years of neglect and vandalism.

In 1963, Reginald and Olive Ryan purchased the deteriorating estate and embarked on a painstaking restoration that would span decades.

The couple raised their five children at Monte Cristo while establishing an antiques and fine art business, eventually opening the property to visitors as a museum.

It was during this period that reports of paranormal encounters began to emerge, helping establish the homestead as one of Junee's best-known tourist attractions.

Despite its eerie reputation, the property boasts remarkable period architecture, ornate interiors and secluded outdoor spaces that offer a glimpse into the lives of its former residents.

Mr Barrett said one of the most atmospheric areas was the grassed courtyard framed by the original dwelling, stables and ballroom.

'This space would have seen relaxed family evenings, the excitement of race day around the stable and all the grandeur of the renowned balls,' he said.

'The stories and moments that would have played out on this turf.'

The agent also highlighted the views from the upper balcony, where visitors can appreciate why the Crawley family chose the elevated location for their residence.

The inclusion of the property's extensive collection of antiques and artwork means the next owner will inherit much of the character the Ryan family spent decades restoring.

On TikTok, some have suggested the homestead would make an ideal bed and breakfast, although its traditional layout could prove unnerving for overnight guests.

'The only creepy thing is the bathrooms are not attached to the individual rooms.

'If you were staying there, you would need to sleep in a room and then walk down a hallway to go to the bathroom in the middle of the night - which might be scary,' Hannah joked.

The chilling stories that earned it a haunted reputation

Over the years, visitors have claimed to encounter ghostly apparitions, unexplained smells, disembodied voices and figures appearing in their rooms at night.

While the paranormal accounts remain unverified, they have become an enduring part of the property's folklore.

Several Australians who had previously visited Monte Cristo shared their experiences online following news of the sale.

'I stayed overnight and I'd never go back! My aunty caught Mrs Crawley in a photo she took in the front sitting room,' one claimed.

Another recalled feeling uncomfortable before they had even entered the building.

'My sister and brother aren't believers and they said it creeped them out. The whole time we were looking around, we felt we were being watched,' they wrote.

'Stunning home, but scary. Yes, it absolutely is haunted. I've been several times and experienced voices, smells and actually seen a spirit,' another claimed.

Others were less concerned by the ghost stories and praised the property for its history and beautifully preserved interiors.

'I've been here - it's such an interesting and amazing experience,' one visitor said.

What will happen to Australia's 'most haunted house'?

The sale has raised questions about the future of one of Junee's most distinctive landmarks and whether its next owner will continue welcoming visitors.

While some Australians are hoping the estate will become a luxury Airbnb or boutique guesthouse, there are concerns that converting it into a private residence could see the town lose an important tourist attraction.

Speaking to the ABC in 2025, Junee Mayor Bob Callow acknowledged the role the property's paranormal reputation had played in attracting visitors.

'It has obviously drawn the attention of people with that sort of interest,' he said.

'It would be hard for the town if someone came and just turned it into a house or an Airbnb. To have it come back as a tourism venue would be the best outcome.'

Whether its next owner is an antiques enthusiast, a history lover or an aspiring hotelier with a fascination for the supernatural, the $1.9million estate offers a property unlike almost any other in Australia.

The question is whether its new residents will be comfortable sharing their home with its alleged former occupants.
